title: The First Kennedy-Nixon Presidential Debate (September 26, 1960)
context: Authentic reconstruction of the historic first televised U.S. presidential debate held at WBBM-TV CBS Studios in Chicago on September 26, 1960, between Senator John F. Kennedy and Vice President Richard M. Nixon, moderated by Howard K. Smith with journalist panelists Sander Vanocur, Charles Warren, and Stuart Novins. Covers opening statements, domestic economic growth versus Soviet competition, federal aid to education and medical care for the aged, civil rights and the federal versus state boundary, fiscal discipline, and closing summations.

metadata.historical_outcome: Watched by an estimated 66-70 million Americans; established television debate framing where Kennedy projected vigor and forward motion while Nixon defended the Eisenhower administration record and goals.

turns.speaker: Howard K. Smith
turns.text: Good evening. The television and radio stations of the United States and their affiliated networks are proud to provide facilities for a discussion of issues in the current political campaign by the two major candidates for the presidency. The candidates need no introduction: the Republican candidate, Vice President Richard M. Nixon, and the Democratic candidate, Senator John F. Kennedy. By agreement between the candidates, tonight's questions are limited to internal or domestic American matters. Each candidate will deliver an eight-minute opening statement, beginning with Senator Kennedy.

turns.speaker: John F. Kennedy
turns.text: Mr. Smith, Mr. Nixon. In the election of 1860, Abraham Lincoln said the question was whether this nation could exist half slave or half free. In the election of 1960, and with the world around us, the question is whether the world will exist half slave or half free, whether it will move in the direction of freedom, in the direction of the road that we are taking, or whether it will move in the direction of slavery. I am not satisfied when the United States had last year the lowest rate of economic growth of any major industrialized society in the world. I am not satisfied until every American enjoys his full constitutional rights. I think it is time America started moving again.

turns.speaker: Richard M. Nixon
turns.text: Mr. Smith, Senator Kennedy. The things that Senator Kennedy has said many of us can agree with. There is no question but that we cannot stand still; we must move forward in this period of the sixties. I subscribe completely to the spirit that Senator Kennedy has expressed tonight, the spirit that the United States should move ahead, and where I disagree is not on the goals for America, but on the means to reach those goals. During the seven and a half years of the Eisenhower administration, we have built more schools, more highways, and more homes, expanded Social Security, and achieved a record national output—all without the kind of big-spending inflation and federal bureaucracy that would undermine free enterprise.

turns.speaker: Howard K. Smith
turns.text: Thank you, gentlemen. We now proceed to questions from our panel of correspondents on the domestic economy and competition with the Soviet Union. Mr. Novins, your question to Senator Kennedy.

turns.speaker: Stuart Novins
turns.text: Senator Kennedy, you have criticized the administration's economic record and argued that the United States must accelerate its annual growth rate to stay ahead of the Soviet Union. Specifically, how do you propose to stimulate faster domestic growth without triggering inflation or unbalancing the federal budget, and why do you believe the Eisenhower-Nixon policies have fallen short?

turns.speaker: John F. Kennedy
turns.text: Because the Soviet Union is producing steel, heavy machinery, and scientists at a rapid rate while our own steel mills are operating at only fifty percent of capacity, and millions of Americans are unemployed or working short weeks. When we have idle factories and idle workers, we cannot afford tight-money, high-interest policies that choke off investment. By restoring full employment, investing in education, research, and modern industrial capacity, and closing tax loopholes rather than raising tax rates, we generate greater economic growth and higher tax revenues to keep the budget balanced without inflation.

turns.speaker: Richard M. Nixon
turns.text: Wait just a minute—let us look at the actual figures rather than campaign slogans. The Soviet Union starts from a vastly lower economic base, roughly forty percent of our gross national product, and even if their percentage growth rate appears high on paper, they are nowhere near catching the United States in total production or living standards. Moreover, when you compare real wages, schools, and disposable family income under Eisenhower versus the Truman years, American families have gained far more real purchasing power because we checked the inflation that ate away Democratic paychecks. Putting government in the driver's seat with billions in new spending would stall, not accelerate, genuine private growth.

turns.speaker: Sander Vanocur
turns.text: Mr. Vice President, Senator Kennedy has said your campaign rests on experience, yet President Eisenhower himself famously paused when asked to name a major idea of yours he had adopted. How directly have your economic and domestic policy recommendations shaped the administration's record on growth and employment?

turns.speaker: Richard M. Nixon
turns.text: The President was obviously engaging in good-natured banter at the end of a long press conference, and as Vice President I have sat in every Cabinet and National Security Council meeting for seven and a half years, advising on economic stabilization, labor policy, and fiscal discipline. What matters to the American voter is not a quick quip, but whether we preserve sound money and private initiative while meeting Soviet competition abroad and at home.

turns.speaker: Howard K. Smith
turns.text: Let us turn to Round 3 on education, teachers' salaries, and medical care for the aged. Mr. Warren, your question.

turns.speaker: Charles Warren
turns.text: Senator Kennedy and Vice President Nixon, both parties acknowledge severe classroom shortages and rising healthcare costs for elderly citizens. Where do you draw the line on federal responsibility for teachers' salaries, school construction, and medical care for senior citizens?

turns.speaker: John F. Kennedy
turns.text: We have nearly two million children attending schools on half-day shifts or in inadequate classrooms, and teachers remain underpaid while our science and engineering needs soar. I favor federal grants to the states that the states themselves may allocate either to school construction or to raising teachers' salaries, without federal interference in local curricula. On medical care for the aged, sixteen million Americans over sixty-five face devastating hospital bills on modest fixed incomes. Placing medical insurance under the Social Security system—paid for during a worker's active career through a small payroll contribution—is fiscally sound, dignified, and preserves every senior citizen's right to choose their own doctor without a demeaning means test.

turns.speaker: Richard M. Nixon
turns.text: Here is the clearest distinction between Senator Kennedy's philosophy and mine. Once the federal government pays teachers' salaries directly from Washington, federal control over local school boards inevitably follows—and I want local communities and states, not a Washington bureau, deciding what our children are taught. Therefore, I support federal aid strictly for school construction and bonds, leaving teachers' salaries to the states. Similarly, Senator Kennedy's compulsory Social Security health plan would force every worker to pay higher taxes while omitting three million elderly Americans not covered by Social Security and threatening the independence of our medical profession. Our voluntary federal-state matching program assists every older citizen who genuinely needs medical help without socializing medicine.

turns.speaker: John F. Kennedy
turns.text: The charge of 'socialized medicine' was hurled against Social Security itself in 1935, and it is no truer today. Under our Social Security bill, the government does not hire doctors or run hospitals; it simply insures hospital bills in retirement just as Social Security insures retirement income, whereas the Vice President's state-by-state charity plan forces elderly citizens to prove poverty before receiving care and leaves states unable to fund their matching share.

turns.speaker: Stuart Novins
turns.text: Turning to civil rights and agricultural surpluses, Vice President Nixon: how far should federal power reach to guarantee equal voting, schooling, and employment rights across the states, and how can farm income be protected without piling up costly government surpluses?

turns.speaker: Richard M. Nixon
turns.text: Civil rights is a moral imperative as well as a national security issue in our competition with communism. Our administration has desegregated Washington, expanded voting enforcement through the Justice Department, and fought for strong civil rights legislation, while recognizing that lasting progress requires moral leadership and federal-state cooperation alongside law enforcement. On agriculture, Democratic high rigid price supports created the very surpluses depressing farm prices today; we must move surpluses abroad to feed hungry nations while letting farmers transition toward market freedom without federal regimentation.

turns.speaker: John F. Kennedy
turns.text: The next President must use the full moral and executive authority of the White House—not merely wait on the courts. A single stroke of the presidential pen can end racial discrimination in federally assisted housing, and the Justice Department must vigorously enforce voting rights so that no American is denied the ballot because of race or color. Meanwhile, on the farm, the administration's policies have driven farm income down while doubling storage costs; supply management that aligns production with demand raises family farm income while reducing surplus stockpiles.

turns.speaker: Sander Vanocur
turns.text: Gentlemen, you both speak of meeting vast domestic needs—education, medical care, civil rights, farm income, and national defense—while avoiding deficit spending. Looking at the federal versus state role, what price tag do your platforms carry for the American taxpayer?

turns.speaker: Richard M. Nixon
turns.text: Our program is carefully costed at approximately four to four and a half billion dollars above current levels, achievable through prudent budget priorities without raising taxes or fueling debt. By contrast, independent estimates of Senator Kennedy's Democratic platform put its new federal spending between thirteen and eighteen billion dollars—which can only be paid by raising taxes on working families, inflating prices, or piling up massive national debt.

turns.speaker: John F. Kennedy
turns.text: Mr. Nixon cites partisan estimates that distort our program. I have consistently pledged a balanced budget except in times of national recession or military emergency, and I believe a growing American economy expanding at four to five percent a year generates the revenues to educate our children, care for our elderly, and strengthen our defenses without raising tax rates.

turns.speaker: Howard K. Smith
turns.text: We have reached the final round for three-minute closing statements. By the toss of the coin, Vice President Nixon will speak first, followed by Senator Kennedy.

turns.speaker: Richard M. Nixon
turns.text: As Senator Kennedy and I conclude this first discussion, let me emphasize once more that we share the same high goals for a strong, free, and growing America. The difference lies in how we get there: whether we rely primarily on centralized federal programs, heavier spending, and expanded Washington bureaucracy, or whether we unleash the creative energy of free citizens, state and local communities, and private enterprise while maintaining sound fiscal policy. We have built a foundation of peace without surrender and prosperity without war; I ask the American people to carry that steady progress forward.

turns.speaker: John F. Kennedy
turns.text: I agree with Vice President Nixon that the goals for a strong America unite us, yet we cannot stand still on the record of the past eight years when Soviet competition and unmet domestic needs demand fresh leadership. If we fail to expand our economy, modernize our schools, secure medical care for the aged under Social Security, and fulfill equal civil rights for every citizen regardless of race, then freedom itself retreats across the globe. Together we can move this country forward again in the 1960s.

turns.speaker: Howard K. Smith
turns.text: Vice President Nixon and Senator Kennedy have concluded their closing statements, joined tonight by correspondents Sander Vanocur, Charles Warren, and Stuart Novins. This concludes the first of the 1960 presidential debates from Chicago. Good night.
